title: Andersons Household Management App
summary: A full-stack Laravel + Livewire app for managing a busy household — trip planning with live route maps, shared meal scheduling, staff/expense tracking, and role-based access for family members, staff, and household admins.
problem: The Anderson household's au pair managed everything manually — cooking schedules, bill payments, task delegation — across a fragmented mix of paper notes and unrelated apps. Coordinating trip logistics, meal planning, staff schedules, and expenses across family members, staff, and admins needed more than a shared calendar: different people needed different slices of the same system — family members shouldn't see staff pay, staff shouldn't see family finances — and admins needed a shortage alert when too many staff were unavailable on the same day.
approach: Ran multiple requirements-gathering meetings with the client (Laurien Stroobants) as part of a team project, coordinating tasks and sprints across the team in Jira, then built a Figma prototype that was reviewed and approved by the client before any code was written. Used MoSCoW prioritization to scope the most important features against a fixed timeline, and weighed non-functional requirements throughout — usability, security, performance, and reliability. Built on Laravel 12 with Livewire 3 (Flux UI) and Tailwind CSS 4, with role-based access (Household Admin, Family Member, Staff, Chef) enforced through Laravel Policies rather than scattered role checks. Personally designed and built the invoice/expense-tracking module and the real-time notification system (WebSocket-based, via Pusher/Laravel Echo) that pushes live updates — trip status, checkpoint arrivals, meal RSVPs — to every connected role without a page refresh. Trips are planned as a route of geocoded checkpoints with live Google Maps previews, document/permit attachments, and per-checkpoint arrival photos, backed by a reusable checkpoints library organized into folders. Address geocoding uses the free Nominatim/OpenStreetMap API.
outcome: Delivered a client-approved Figma prototype before development began, then shipped as a live production app handling trips, meals, invoices, staff availability, and household scheduling for four distinct roles, with automated checkpoint-arrival and trip-overdue reminders running as scheduled console commands.
highlights: Client Collaboration: Ran multiple requirements meetings and delivered a Figma prototype approved by the client before development began.
Personally Built: The invoice/expense-tracking module and the real-time WebSocket notification system (Pusher/Laravel Echo).
MoSCoW Prioritization: Scoped must-have features against a fixed academic timeline.
Non-Functional Requirements: Usability, security, performance, and reliability considered throughout, not just feature checklist.
Live production deployment, not just a local demo — role-based access across 4 roles enforced via Laravel Policies.
Live Google Maps route previews over geocoded trip checkpoints; tested with Pest 4, including CI via GitHub Actions.

title: MotoGP Tickets
summary: A course project built for my .NET Development course — a layered ASP.NET Core Web API and a React frontend for browsing MotoGP races and booking tickets.
problem: This was a course project for my .NET Development course, built to practice a properly layered ASP.NET Core API rather than a single monolithic project — separating contracts, domain logic, and infrastructure so each layer could be tested and changed independently, with a real React frontend consuming it.
approach: Structured the API into four layers: MotoGP.Api (controllers, AutoMapper profiles, Program.cs), MotoGP.Contracts (DTOs only), MotoGP.Domain (POCO entities, pagination helper, Strategy-pattern interfaces), and MotoGP.Infrastructure (EF Core DbContext, migrations, Repositories, seeders) — following the Repository pattern throughout. Used Auth0 JWT auth to gate admin-only endpoints (listing all tickets, marking a ticket paid) while keeping ticket ordering public. Documented every endpoint via Swagger, and covered all four layers with MSTest unit tests using Moq. Built a separate React + Vite client that talks to the API over Axios, with the API base URL driven by an environment variable so it can point at either a local or deployed API.
outcome: Delivered a working end-to-end booking flow — browsing races and placing a ticket order — backed by a SQL Server database that migrates and seeds automatically on first run, with a full MSTest suite passing across all layers.
highlights: Course Project: Built for my .NET Development course.
4-Layer Architecture: Api, Contracts, Domain, and Infrastructure layers kept strictly separated via the Repository pattern.
Auth0 JWT: Admin-only endpoints gated behind token auth while order placement stays public.
Tested: MSTest + Moq unit tests across all four layers, all passing.
Decoupled Frontend: React/Vite client talking to the API over Axios, independently deployable.

title: Pro Cycling WorldTour Stage Analytics
summary: An automated multi-source extraction pipeline and exploratory analysis investigating internationalization, podium concentration, and team composition across 995 Grand Tour stage finishes.
problem: WorldTour race classifications are scattered across disparate HTML tables and paginated sports portals with inconsistent athlete naming conventions. Investigating whether elite cycling is genuinely globalized or dominated by traditional European feeder nations required an automated, resilient extraction pipeline spanning 15 tour editions (2021–2025).
approach: Engineered an object-oriented Python scraper using cloudscraper and BeautifulSoup4 with custom browser headers, timeouts, and polite request delays to navigate anti-bot protections. Parsed HTML tables and CSS flag classes across Wikipedia and FirstCycling, standardizing 54 national identities into validated 3-letter UCI codes. Cached the resulting 995-row dataset locally to decouple downstream analytics from network dependencies.
outcome: Delivered a zero-loss analytical pipeline evaluating five competitive hypotheses. Demonstrated that while stage racing maintains a broad international baseline (12–18 nations per tour in the top 10), top-5 podium finishes remain concentrated, with France (13.9%) and Belgium (11.3%) occupying more than a quarter of all top results.
highlights: 995 Clean Records: Extracted 657 Wikipedia and 338 FirstCycling finishes with 0 missing values.
Roster Diversity as a Floor-Raiser: Roster diversity strongly correlates with total top-10 finish volume (r = 0.78), serving as a consistency strategy rather than an individual podium guarantee.
Host Bias: Italian and French tours show a 22–24% home rider finish share, dropping to 6.7% in the Tour de Suisse.

title: Vehicle Breakdown Classification
summary: A collaborative predictive maintenance pipeline and ablation study optimizing tree-based ensembles for highly imbalanced failure data.
problem: Predicting vehicle mechanical failures requires navigating extreme class imbalance (a 5:1 ratio of healthy to broken-down cars). Furthermore, traditional accuracy is a dangerous metric for predictive maintenance: a False Negative (missing a breakdown) results in stranded drivers and costly engine failure, whereas a False Positive is merely an unnecessary inspection.
approach: Working within a team of 3, we engineered a leakage-free data pipeline utilizing IQR winsorization and median imputation fitted strictly on training splits. To determine the best modeling strategy, I conducted an ablation study evaluating four Random Forest architectures. We optimized the decision threshold to maximize the F2-score (weighing Recall twice as heavily as Precision) and implemented a Balanced Random Forest with bootstrap sampling to inherently penalize the majority class.
outcome: The study yielded a highly valuable insight: algorithm-level balancing on raw data significantly outperformed manual feature engineering, which introduced noise. The final Balanced Random Forest achieved an 87% Recall rate and a 0.93 OOB ROC-AUC locally, generalizing successfully to achieve a 0.839 score on the Kaggle hold-out test set.
highlights: Kaggle Validated: Scored 0.839 on the competition leaderboard, proving strong generalization on unseen data.
Business-Aligned Metrics: Shifted evaluation from raw Accuracy to F2-Score and PR-AUC to minimize expensive False Negatives.
Team Collaboration: Coordinated preprocessing, model selection, and validation workflows across a 3-person team.

title: Lizard Species Image Classification
summary: An end-to-end computer vision pipeline utilizing transfer learning, test-time augmentation, and fine-tuned EfficientNet architectures for a multi-class Kaggle competition.
problem: The challenge required classifying 7 visually similar lizard species for a Kaggle competition using a highly constrained dataset of only 1,334 training images. Training deep neural networks from scratch on small datasets risks severe overfitting, necessitating aggressive regularization, transfer learning, and domain-specific spatial priors to ensure generalization to unseen test data.
approach: Engineered a two-phase TensorFlow pipeline leveraging an EfficientNetV2-S backbone for its parameter efficiency. Trained a custom classification head before selectively fine-tuning the top 40 layers. Crucially, Batch Normalization layers were frozen during fine-tuning to prevent feature degradation. Applied in-model Keras augmentations while intentionally excluding vertical flips to preserve natural lizard orientation.
outcome: The two-phase architecture stabilized learning and eliminated the validation loss degradation typically seen in small-dataset fine-tuning. The model achieved a 0.764 Macro F1-score on the validation split. By implementing Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) and label smoothing (0.1), the final submission secured an estimated 1–2% performance boost on the Kaggle leaderboard.
highlights: Strategic Fine-Tuning: Froze 110 BatchNorm layers during Phase 2 to prevent catastrophic forgetting and overfitting.
Robust Inference: Implemented Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) to average predictions across multiple augmented versions of test images.
Mixed Precision: Utilized mixed_float16 policies to maximize GPU memory efficiency and accelerate training times.

title: Industrial Bottling Analytics: End-to-End Qlik Sense Dashboard
summary: A 3-tier operational dashboard built to transform plant telemetry into clear, actionable reporting using advanced chart selection and interactive UI controls.
problem: Industrial bottling lines produce high-density operational data across shift outputs, flavor recipes, and unexpected machine stops. The objective was to design a clean, intuitive multi-sheet dashboard in Qlik Sense that translates raw production telemetry into fast operational insights — ensuring operators and managers can identify line bottlenecks without navigating through clutter.
approach: Structured the reporting into a three-tier dashboard flow: an Executive Summary sheet surfacing headline throughput, total plant uptime vs. downtime, flavor volume distribution, and median downtime limits; an Operational Trends sheet highlighting day-to-day production patterns alongside ranked downtime reasons; and a Batch Details sheet for flavor-group comparisons and granular batch auditing down to individual production runs. Selected chart types for precise encoding — horizontal gauge bars with green/amber/red color segments to flag downtime against plant benchmarks, dual-layer area charts with dynamic reference lines comparing daily production volume to average downtime, and conditional background colors on pivot tables to flag batches exceeding acceptable downtime limits. Built dynamic button controls driven by variables (vTopN) to toggle between Top 3 and Top 5 downtime drivers in real time, and applied Set Analysis ({1}) to isolate flavor-group donut charts (cola vs. fruit) as fixed benchmarks that stay static regardless of global user selections.
outcome: Delivered a polished, responsive manufacturing dashboard providing full line visibility across 41 production cycles, enabling floor supervisors to track throughput targets, quickly identify leading downtime causes, and drill directly into problematic batches and downtime reasons.
highlights: Three-Tier Reporting: Executive Summary, Operational Trends, and Batch Details sheets structured for progressively deeper drill-down.
Set Analysis: Used {1} expressions to lock flavor-group donut charts as fixed benchmarks, unaffected by global filter selections.
Dynamic Variable Controls: Built a vTopN-driven button toggle to switch between Top 3 and Top 5 downtime drivers in real time.
Precise Visual Encoding: Color-thresholded gauge bars, dual-layer area charts with reference lines, and conditional pivot-table formatting to flag downtime outliers at a glance.
